insights: Working in ZMod q: q ∣ 2^p−1 ⟺ (2:ZMod q)^p = 1; orderOf 2 divides p, and equals p (order 1 forces q ∣ 1). This is the whole engine for the mod-2p restriction.
p = 2 genuinely breaks both restrictions (2^2−1=3, 3≢1 mod 4, 3≢±1 mod 8); the odd-prime hypothesis is used twice — coprimality of 2,p and writing 2 as a square — so it is necessary not cosmetic.
Since (2:ZMod q)^p=1 with p odd, 2 = 2^{p+1} is an even power = (2^{(p+1)/2})², giving IsSquare(2) for free with no Legendre-symbol computation.
Order of 2 in ZMod q equals p exactly (divides prime p, not 1 since 2≠1 in ZMod q), the shared engine for both congruences
Coprimality of 2 and p (p odd) upgrades p∣q−1 to 2p∣q−1 via Nat.Coprime.mul_dvd_of_dvd_of_dvd
p=2k+1 odd gives 2=2·2^p=(2^{k+1})² in ZMod q, so 2 is a QR — ZMod.exists_sq_eq_two_iff closes to q%8∈{1,7}
Restrictions genuinely fail at p=2 (M_2=3), so odd-prime hypothesis is necessary not cosmetic
nextSteps: Generalize to base a: prime factors of a^p−1 (q∤a) satisfy q ≡ 1 mod 2p via orderOf a = p; characterize QR of a mod q for the residue condition.
Package into a trial-division bound: smallest prime factor of composite 2^p−1 is ≥ 2p+1; enumerate admissible residue classes mod 8p.
